summary: This document defines a collection of common data types for the YANG data modeling language, including new type definitions. It obsoletes RFC 6991.

plainLanguage.summary: YANG is the language used to describe the configuration and state of network devices. It only has a few built-in kinds of value, so a shared library of common types saves every model from inventing its own. This document is that library: counters, gauges, dates and times, addresses, prefixes, port numbers, domain names, UUIDs and more, split into a general module and one for the Internet protocol suite.

questions: what is the yang counter32 type
subtitle: A shared library of data types that YANG models can reuse for counters, times, addresses and more.

tldr.problem: YANG comes with only a small set of built-in data types, so every model that needs a counter, a timestamp, an IP address or a port number would otherwise define its own version of it, and the definitions would drift apart.
tldr.mechanism: The document publishes two YANG modules. ietf-yang-types holds generally useful types such as counters, gauges, date and time values and common string formats, and ietf-inet-types holds types for the Internet Protocol suite such as addresses, prefixes, domain names, URIs and port numbers.
tldr.outcome: This revision replaced RFC 6991. It adds date, time and duration types, a language-tag type, aligns the yang-identifier definition with YANG 1.1 and improves several patterns.

today: RFC 9911 is a Proposed Standard that replaced RFC 6991, which had replaced RFC 6021. The metadata for this RFC lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Two Shared YANG Modules
sections.content:
YANG is a data modeling language used to model configuration and state data manipulated by the Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF). The language supports a small set of built-in data types and provides mechanisms to derive other types from the built-in types.

This document defines a collection of common data types, organized into two YANG modules. The ietf-yang-types module defines generally useful data types such as types for counters and gauges, types related to date and time, and types for common string values, for example UUIDs, dotted-quad notation and language tags. The ietf-inet-types module defines data types relevant to the Internet Protocol suite, such as types related to IP addresses, types for domain name, host name, URI and email, and types for values in common protocol fields such as port numbers.

The initial version of these modules was published as RFC 6021. The first revision of RFC 6021, published as RFC 6991, added several type definitions. This second revision adds further new type definitions and addresses two errata. The yang-identifier definition has been aligned with YANG 1.1, and some pattern statements have been improved. Additional type definitions may be added in the future by submitting proposals to the NETMOD Working Group.
sections.plainLanguage: YANG is the language used to describe the configuration and state of network devices. It only has a few built-in kinds of value, so a shared library of common types saves every model from inventing its own.

sections.title: The Type Catalogue and the SNMP Equivalents
sections.content:
Two tables list every type in the ietf-yang-types module and in the ietf-inet-types module. For each type the table gives its name, the base type it was derived from, and the RFC that introduced it.

The ietf-yang-types module holds counter32 and zero-based-counter32, both from uint32; counter64 and zero-based-counter64, both from uint64; gauge32 and gauge64; object-identifier and object-identifier-128; date-and-time and the new date, date-no-zone, time and time-no-zone; the duration types hours32, minutes32, seconds32, centiseconds32, milliseconds32, microseconds32, microseconds64, nanoseconds32 and nanoseconds64; timeticks and timestamp; phys-address and mac-address; xpath1.0; hex-string, uuid and dotted-quad; language-tag; and yang-identifier.

The ietf-inet-types module holds ip-version, dscp, ipv6-flow-label, port-number, protocol-number, upper-layer-protocol-number and as-number; ip-address with the ipv4-address and ipv6-address variants, the no-zone and link-local variants, and the address-and-prefix variants; ip-prefix with its ipv4-prefix and ipv6-prefix variants; domain-name and host-name; host; uri; and email-address.

Some types have an equivalent Structure of Management Information Version 2 data type. A YANG type is equivalent to an SMIv2 type if the two have the same set of values and the semantics of those values are equivalent. Two tables list these pairs, so that a value written for a management system that uses SNMP means the same thing when it is carried in YANG.
sections.plainLanguage: The document lists every type with the built-in type it is built from and the RFC that first shipped it. It also lists the SNMP types that mean exactly the same thing, so a value keeps its meaning when it moves between the two worlds.

sections.title: The ietf-yang-types Module
sections.content:
The counter types describe numbers that only go up. The counter32 type represents a non-negative integer that increases monotonically until it reaches 2^32-1, 4294967295 in decimal, when it wraps around and starts again from zero. A counter has no defined initial value, so a single value of a counter has, in general, no information content. Discontinuities normally occur when the management system is re-initialized, and a schema node should be defined to indicate the last discontinuity if one happens at other times. The counter32 type should not be used for configuration nodes, and a default statement should not be used with it.

The gauge types are for numbers that move up and down. The gauge32 type represents a non-negative integer which may increase or decrease but never exceeds 2^32-1, 4294967295 in decimal, and never falls below 0. The gauge64 type is the same with a maximum of 2^64-1, 18446744073709551615. The zero-based counter variants count from zero rather than from one.

The time types are the largest change in this revision. The date-and-time type is a profile of the ISO 8601 standard for dates and times using the Gregorian calendar, defined by the date-time production in Section 5.6 of RFC 3339 and the update in Section 2 of RFC 9557. The value 60 for seconds is allowed only in the case of leap seconds. The type does not allow negative years. The time offset Z means the value is reported in UTC and the local time zone reference point is unknown, while an offset of +00:00 means it is reported in UTC and the local reference point is known to be UTC.

The new date type represents a time interval of the length of a day, 24 hours, with an optional time zone offset, and date-no-zone is the same without the offset. The new time type represents an instance of time of zero duration that recurs every day, again with an optional offset, and time-no-zone is the same without it. The duration types hours32, minutes32, seconds32, centiseconds32, milliseconds32, microseconds32 and nanoseconds32 are based on int32, and microseconds64 and nanoseconds64 on int64.

The string types are simple formats with a canonical spelling. The hex-string type is octets written as hex digits separated by colons, canonically in lowercase. The uuid type is the string representation of a UUID defined in RFC 9562, for example f81d4fae-7dec-11d0-a765-00a0c91e6bf6, again canonically in lowercase. The dotted-quad type is an unsigned 32-bit number written as four decimal octets separated by full stops. The language-tag type is a language tag according to RFC 5646, canonically in lowercase. The yang-identifier type is a YANG identifier as defined by the identifier rule in Section 14 of RFC 7950: it must start with an alphabetic character or an underscore, followed by any sequence of alphabetic or numeric characters, underscores, hyphens or dots.
sections.plainLanguage: The counters are for things that only count up and wrap around at the end of their range. The gauges are for numbers that move up and down within fixed limits. The time types cover a whole date and time, a date on its own, a time of day on its own, and durations from hours down to nanoseconds. The string types fix one spelling for each format so that two systems write the same value the same way.

sections.title: The ietf-inet-types Module
sections.content:
The ietf-inet-types module holds the types that describe values from the Internet protocol suite.

An IPv4 address is written in dotted-quad notation and may carry a zone index after a percent sign, which disambiguates identical address values; for link-local addresses the zone is typically the interface index or name, and if no zone is given the device's default zone is used. The canonical form of the zone index is numerical. The ip-address type is a union of the IPv4 and IPv6 forms, and the variants without a zone and the link-local variants narrow it further.

The ip-prefix type is a union of the IPv4 and IPv6 prefix forms, and the address-and-prefix types pair an address with the length of its prefix.

The domain-name type represents a DNS domain name and should be fully qualified whenever possible. It does not support wildcards or classless in-addr.arpa delegations. Its length is 1 to 253 characters, which follows from the fact that the DNS encoding of names is limited to 255 characters, made up of labels each prefixed by a length byte plus a trailing NUL byte. Internet domain names are only loosely specified, so the pattern is intended to allow current practice and some possible future expansion. A schema node representing a host name should use the host-name type instead. The description clause of a node using the domain-name type must say when and how the name is resolved to IP addresses, and the resolution may need to query several DNS records, such as A for IPv4 and AAAA for IPv6. Domain names use ASCII encoding and their canonical form is lowercase; internationalized domain names must be A-labels.

The port-number type represents a 16-bit port number of an Internet transport-layer protocol such as UDP, TCP, DCCP or SCTP, with a range of 0 to 65535. Port numbers are assigned by IANA, and the value zero is reserved, so it can be excluded by subtyping where it makes no sense.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the types for values that come from the network itself: addresses, prefixes, host names, web addresses and port numbers. Each one fixes the accepted spelling and the canonical spelling, and says what the value means, for example that a port number of zero is reserved.

sections.title: What This Revision Changes
sections.content:
The module carries its own revision history. The initial revision of 2010-09-24 shipped in RFC 6021. The revision of 2013-07-15, shipped in RFC 6991, added the yang-identifier, hex-string, uuid and dotted-quad types.

The revision in this document, dated 2025-12-22, adds the date, date-no-zone, time and time-no-zone types, the duration types hours32, minutes32, seconds32, centiseconds32, milliseconds32, microseconds32, microseconds64, nanoseconds32 and nanoseconds64, and the language-tag type. It aligns the yang-identifier definition with YANG 1.1, makes the time types support the representation of leap seconds, aligns the representation of time zone offsets with RFC 9557, and improves several description and pattern statements.

The change to yang-identifier matters in one respect. In RFC 6991 the definition excluded all identifiers starting with any combination of the lowercase or uppercase character sequence xml, as YANG 1 required. The new definition, following YANG 1.1, drops that exclusion, though the restriction still applies when the type is used in a YANG 1 context.
sections.plainLanguage: This edition adds the date, time and duration types and a language tag type, brings the identifier type in line with the current version of YANG, and tidies up several of the patterns that decide what a valid value looks like.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The document reuses the URIs for ietf-yang-types and ietf-inet-types in the IETF XML Registry. Following the format of RFC 6020, the registrations are:

  • Name ietf-yang-types, namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-yang-types, prefix yang, reference RFC 9911.
  • Name ietf-inet-types, namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-inet-types, prefix inet, reference RFC 9911.

IANA has updated the YANG Module Names registry to point at this document instead of RFC 6991 for both modules.
sections.plainLanguage: The two module names and their namespaces are recorded in the official list, so that no one else uses them for something else.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document defines common data types using the YANG data modeling language. The definitions themselves have no security impact on the Internet, but the usage of these definitions in concrete YANG modules might have. The security considerations spelled out in the YANG specification apply for this document as well.
sections.plainLanguage: The types themselves carry no risk. What a model does with the values it holds is where the risk lies, and that is covered by the rules of YANG itself.

May rise or fall, between 0 and 2^32-1
May rise or fall, between 0 and 2^64-1

cells: An IPv4 address in dotted-quad notation, with an optional zone index
Either an IPv4 or an IPv6 address
Either an IPv4 or an IPv6 prefix
A DNS domain name, 1 to 253 characters, ASCII
A host name, with a stricter syntax
